title: State Minimisation
quickIdea: Two states are equivalent when no input sequence can tell them apart. Merge them and the state count falls, which usually falls below a power of two and so removes a flip-flop.
remember: Equivalent states: for every input they give the same output, and their next states are the same or themselves equivalent. The definition is recursive, which is why the algorithm is iterative.

Partition refinement: start by grouping states by their output. Then split any group whose members go to different groups on some input. Repeat until nothing splits. Each surviving group is one state.
The implication table does the same job by hand: cross out a pair whose outputs differ, then cross out a pair that implies a crossed-out pair, and repeat.
Minimisation is worth doing because the flip-flop count is ceil(log2 number of states): going from 5 states to 4 saves a flip-flop, going from 9 to 8 saves one, and going from 8 to 4 saves one more.
Incompletely specified machines break the transitivity of equivalence, so the partition method does not apply unchanged and the problem becomes finding a maximum compatible set.
Row matching, which merges only states with identical next-state and output rows, is a first pass and not a substitute for refinement.

example.prompt: Nine states A to I are reduced to four by the standard example: A, D and G merge, B, C and F merge, E and H merge, and I stands alone. How many flip-flops does each version need?
example.work: Nine states need ceil(log2 9) = 4 flip-flops. Four states need ceil(log2 4) = 2. The reduction therefore saves two flip-flops, and it also shrinks the combinational logic that decodes the states.
example.answer: Four flip-flops before, two after. The nine-to-four reduction is the worked example in Auburn ELEC 2200 Lecture 7.

gateAngle: GATE asks two things: the minimum number of states for a specification, and the number of flip-flops after reduction. The first needs the essential-memory argument, the second needs the partition.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A four-state machine has outputs 0, 0, 1, 1 for states A, B, C, D. A and B both go to C on input 0 and to D on input 1; C and D both go to A on 0 and to B on 1. What is the minimum number of states?
variations.answer: Two. A and B are equivalent, and so are C and D, because each pair agrees on outputs and their next states fall in the same pair.
variations.why: The first partition is {A, B} and {C, D}. The refinement test passes because A and B both go to the {C, D} group on either input, so nothing splits.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why is the equivalence relation on states not transitive when the machine has don't-care outputs?
variations.answer: Two states can be compatible through a third without being compatible with each other, because a don't care matches anything. Compatibility is therefore not an equivalence relation, and the clean partition argument fails.
variations.why: This is why the incompletely specified case needs maximum compatible sets, which is a harder problem. GATE's questions are fully specified for exactly this reason.

trap.what: Merging two states that have the same output but different next states.
trap.why: Equivalence needs both conditions. Matching outputs is only the first partition; the next-state condition is what the refinement steps test, and skipping it merges states that a later input can distinguish.
trap.counterexample: Two states both outputting 0 but going to different states on input 0 look mergeable in the first partition. If those destinations differ in output, the second partition splits them, and merging them would change the machine's behaviour.

check.question: A machine has 6 states. After minimisation it has 4. How many flip-flops are saved?
check.explanation: The saving is not proportional to the states removed; it is the difference of two logarithms. Going from 8 to 5 states saves nothing, because both need three flip-flops.

sourceLine: The equivalent-state definition, the implication table, the nine-to-four worked reduction and the flip-flop count: Auburn ELEC 2200 Lecture 7 (English, read in full). The state-reduction step in the synthesis procedure and the remark that it is easy to tell when two states are not equivalent but hard to tell when they are: IIT Bombay CS 226 Lecture 7 (English, read in full). No verified GATE CSE question of this topic is decided by a reduction alone, which is why this card carries none.
